idiom_name: TPL: Parallel.ForEachAsync / Task.Run + Task.WhenAll over the ThreadPool
implementation_notes: The .NET ThreadPool is the worker set and the TPL supplies dispatch and aggregation: Task.Run queues one subtask per call and Task.WhenAll is the join whose result array carries the partials in submission order, while Parallel.ForEachAsync (a .NET 6+ API) runs the body for each item with at most Environment.ProcessorCount operations in flight and takes a CancellationToken for the master's cancellation policy. Parallel.ForEachAsync is the asynchronous replacement for the blocking Parallel.For/ForEach and should be preferred whenever the body awaits; Channel<T> is the primitive when work arrives over time or needs back-pressure, with one reader task per worker.
pitfalls: Parallel.ForEachAsync caps concurrency at Environment.ProcessorCount, so wrapping the body in blocking calls (.Result, .Wait(), Thread.Sleep) starves the pool instead of adding parallelism.
Collecting results into a plain List<T> from parallel bodies corrupts it; use ConcurrentBag<T>, index the result array, or await Task.WhenAll and reduce in submission order.
A cancelled token makes ForEachAsync throw OperationCanceledException and discards the remaining iterations - partial results must be designed for, not assumed.
